facts.claim: Queen Victoria married Prince Albert on 10 February 1840; Britannica lists 12 bridesmaids, who also wore white, and says her 18-foot train was carried by her bridesmaids, who struggled to shepherd it down the aisle.
facts.quote: Victoria wore a white satin gown that featured delicate British-made lace, a wreath of orange blossoms, and an 18-foot-long train (which her bridesmaids struggled to shepherd down the aisle). ... 12: Victoria's bridesmaids (who also wore white)
facts.conflicts: Re-checked the pillar's fact_301: confirmed. The page also says royals had typically married in private ceremonies in state robes; it does not explain why bridesmaids matched.

facts.claim: A Dictionary of Superstitions (Opie and Tatem, Oxford Reference) records the belief that being a bridesmaid too many times is unlucky, citing 1834 (Dalyell, Scotland), 1898 ('Three times a bridesmaid, never a bride') and twentieth-century schoolgirl informants.
facts.quote: 1834 DALYELL Darker Superstitions of Scotland 292. It is yet held ominous for any damsel to officiate frequently as bridesmaid ... Superstition assigns perpetual celibacy as her lot. 1898 Weekly Scotsman Christmas Number 7. Three times a bridesmaid, never a bride.
facts.conflicts: Read as the Oxford Reference search excerpt (entry 'BRIDESMAID too many times'); full entry is subscription-only.

facts.claim: The Oxford Dictionary of Proverbs dates 'Always a bridesmaid, never a bride' with quotations from 1882 ('Always a maiden [bridal attendant], never a wife'), 1903 and a 1917 song, and says the 'often a bridesmaid' version was popularised by mouthwash advertisements from the 1920s.
facts.quote: Used of someone who seems fated to be always the runner-up or second best. The version with often (quot. 1951) was popularized in a series of advertisements from the 1920s onwards for a brand of mouthwash ... 1882 e. m. ingraham Bond & Free i. Always a maiden [bridal attendant], never a wife. 1903 v. s. lean Collectanea II. 81 Three times bridesmaid, never a bride. 1917 leigh, collins, & morris 'Why am I always the Bridesmaid?' (song)
facts.conflicts: Search excerpt only. Oxford Reference overview 'bride' calls it a late 19th-century saying recording the belief that being a bridesmaid too often is unlucky for one's own chances of marriage.

facts.claim: royal.uk: Queen Victoria married at St James's Palace Chapel on 10 February 1840; she sketched the simple white dress, trimmed with sprays of roses, worn by her dozen bridesmaids, and gave the sketch to her Mistress of the Robes, the Duchess of Sutherland, who supervised the making of the dresses.
facts.quote: Married at St James' Palace Chapel ... Queen Victoria sketched this simple white dress design, trimmed with sprays of roses worn by her dozen bridesmaids. This sketch was given to her Mistress of the Robes, The Duchess of Sutherland, who supervised the making of the dresses.
facts.conflicts: Official royal household site. Note: a royal.uk 'Royal wedding traditions' search snippet gives '10 April 1840'; the timeline and Britannica give 10 February 1840. Use 10 February.

facts.claim: Royal Collection Trust: Queen Victoria herself designed the dresses worn by her twelve bridesmaids, who were all the eldest daughters of peers (collection item RCIN 980021, c. 1840).
facts.quote: Queen Victoria herself undertook the design for the dresses worn by her twelve bridesmaids, who were all the eldest daughters of peers. She outlined a simple ...
facts.conflicts: Quote is the rct.uk text as shown in the search result for this page (apify web-search, 2026-11-10); the page body renders client-side and did not return in the fetch. Wording matches fact_04 (royal.uk).

facts.claim: V&A: Prince Albert designed an eagle-shaped turquoise brooch as a gift for Queen Victoria's twelve train bearers at their 1840 wedding, taken from the heraldic German eagle; the turquoise suggests forget-me-nots and the pearls represent true love.
facts.quote: Perhaps the most notable bridegroom of the 19th century, Prince Albert, designed an eagle shaped turquoise brooch as a gift to Queen Victoria's twelve train bearers at their wedding. The design is taken from the heraldic German eagle. Although the turquoise and pearls don't have an enormous financial value, the blue of the stones suggests forget-me-nots, whilst the pearls represent true love.
facts.conflicts: Museum article (schema has no museum type). The brooch pictured is in the British Museum, not the V&A.

facts.claim: V&A: the nineteenth century, when notions of wedding customs began to solidify, often saw groups of eight or twelve girls or women accompanying and supporting the bride; bridesmaids were often young sisters and cousins of the bride and groom, as well as female friends.
facts.quote: The nineteenth century, where our notions of wedding customs began to solidify, often saw groups of eight or twelve girls or women accompanying and supporting the bride. Bridesmaids were often the young sisters and cousins of the bride and groom, as well as female friends.

facts.claim: V&A: traditionally, bridesmaids supplied their own dresses but were given a piece of jewellery, such as a brooch or locket, as a gift or souvenir; in the UK the groom customarily gave the gifts, while Vogue noted that nineteenth-century American brides gave gifts to their own bridesmaids.
facts.quote: Traditionally, bridesmaids supplied their own dresses, but were offered a piece of jewellery as a gift or souvenir of the wedding. ... As the groom customarily gave gifts to the bridesmaids ... One point of etiquette, according to Vogue, was that 19th century American women would give gifts to their own bridesmaids, whereas this was the duty of the groom in the United Kingdom.

facts.claim: V&A: at the 1884 wedding of Val Prinsep and Florence Leyland the bridesmaids were dressed in canary yellow and wore brooches engraved 'Val and Flo', a gift of the groom; a V&A design sheet for the Gibson wedding specifies six matching bridesmaids' brooches in silver.
facts.quote: The bridesmaids were smartly dressed in canary yellow and wore brooches engraved 'Val and Flo', a gift of the groom. ... The first is annotated 'bridesmaids', with a design marked 'No. 1', specifying that six brooches were required in silver.
facts.conflicts: Shows coordinated dress and matching gifts in the 1880s and 1860s; the V&A does not give a reason for bridesmaids dressing alike.

facts.claim: The Oxford Classical Dictionary (4th ed.) describes the Roman wedding: friends and clients gathered in the bride's father's house, words of consent were spoken, and the matron of honour (pronuba) performed the ceremony of linking the bride's and bridegroom's right hands (dextrarum iunctio).
facts.quote: Friends and clients of both families gathered in the bride's father's house: the bridegroom arrived, words of consent were spoken, and the matron of honour ( pronuba ) performed the ceremony of linking bride's and bridegroom's right hands ( dextrarum iunctio ).
facts.conflicts: Oxford Reference search excerpt (search 'matron of honour' and 'pronuba'), entry 'marriage ceremonies' by Sourvinou-Inwood and Williams. The Oxford Dictionary of the Classical World and Oxford Companion to Classical Literature excerpts say the same ('their hands were linked by the matron of honour'). No source read links the Roman pronuba directly to the modern bridesmaid or matron of honour: do not state a line of descent.

facts.claim: The Oxford Companion to Classical Literature adds that after the hand-linking the Roman bride was conducted to her husband's house by three boys (excerpt truncated after 'three').
facts.quote: Friends gathered in the bride's father's house, both bride and groom spoke words of consent and their hands were linked by the matron of honour. The bride was conducted to the husband's house by three...
facts.conflicts: Excerpt is cut off after 'three'; do not name who the three were from this source. Claim to use: 'the matron of honour linked the couple's hands'.

The V&A notes that at the time it was fashionable for younger bridesmaids and pageboys to wear outfits based on historic or national costume; this one copies English styles of the 1630s and 1640s.

facts.quote: attended wedding feasts where bridesmaids danced and male guests might talk with other female guests ( Isaeus 8.18 ; Aristophanes, Acharnians 1056).

insider_details.detail: Victoria's twelve bridesmaids carried an 18-foot train and found it hard going down the aisle: a long train or cathedral veil today needs one or two named attendants briefed and rehearsed on the actual aisle, steps and turns of the ceremony venue.

Albert gave each of Victoria's twelve bridesmaids a matching eagle brooch he designed himself, and Victorian grooms commonly chose gifts reflecting the couple's initials or crest: a personalised keepsake for each attendant is a thank-you with real historical pedigree, and it travels easily to an overseas wedding.

Victorian bridesmaids supplied their own dresses while the couple gave the gift: who pays for dresses and travel has always been a conversation, so raise it with your attendants early and in person, before anyone books.

In 1840 the Queen sketched one dress for all twelve and her Mistress of the Robes oversaw the making: when attendants are scattered across cities, one trusted person coordinating fittings is a practice with a royal precedent.

Both Cambridge and Oxford treat the maid of honour as the chief bridesmaid and the matron of honour as the married equivalent, so the lead attendant's title can simply follow the couple's preference; the role itself is the same lead-helper job.

The core definition of a bridesmaid is someone who helps the bride before and during the ceremony, which is the frame for the roles section: helping with plans in the months before, then getting ready, the bouquet and the processional on the day.
Seating guests is a defined groomsman (UK: usher) duty; in a mixed party, bridesmen and groomswomen can share those on-the-day jobs, which is living practice rather than dictionary usage.

When inviting attendants to travel, ask early enough for each person to check their passport has at least six months' validity beyond the trip and to arrange their own travel insurance that covers every country on the route, including stopovers, and cancellation if plans change.
Share one wedding-week itinerary with the whole party and suggest they keep hard copies of flights, accommodation and event bookings; attendants declare any health conditions to their own insurer.
